newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Slower German economy no help to EMU hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Slower German economy no help to EMU hopes.

text.p: German economic growth slowed moderately in the first quarter of 1997, the Federal Statistics Office said on Thursday, raising fresh questions on whether Germany will be able to qualify for European monetary union.

The statistics office said growth in gross domestic product (GDP) slowed to 1.4 percent year-on-year in the first quarter of this year from 1.9 percent in the fourth quarter of last year and 2.3 percent in the third quarter of 1996.
Compared with the previous quarter, however, GDP grew 0.5 percent.

Economists said seasonal factors depressed GDP growth substantially, making it appear worse than it really was, but still said Germany faces an uphill fight to reach the government's 2.5 percent growth forecast for the whole year.

"I think the full year-year 1997 growth will be slightly less than the government's growth forecast of 2.5 percent and that could add to the government's budget problems," said Lothar Hessler, bond analyst at Trinkaus & Burkhardt.
Calculations based on Bundesbank data, corrected for the fact that this year's first quarter had three fewer workdays than last year's, show year-on-year growth was 2.8 percent.
Germany is struggling to reduce its budget deficit to three percent of GDP as mandated by the Maastricht Treaty for nations hoping to join EMU in January 1999.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel has repeatedly said Germany will be able to meet that goal, but bases that forecast on the economy growing at a 2.5 percent pace.
Slow economic growth eats into tax revenues and forces the government to pay out more in unemployment aid.
In west Germany, the economy grew 1.2 percent year-on-year while in east Germany it expanded 2.8 percent from the first quarter of 1996, the statistics office said.
Economists said the economy remains sluggish largely because consumers, unnerved by record high unemployment levels, are reluctant to spend.
With demand weak, a second major pillar of the economy, investment, has also failed to provide much support.
Only exports, helped by a weaker mark, have given the economy much of a lift in recent months.
Not all economists, however, saw the GDP report as proof that the economy will fail to recover in time to help Bonn qualify for EMU.
Some said the 0.5 percent quarter-on-quarter growth gave a better view of the economy's underlying strength.
"We have an unusual calendar in the first quarter," said Uwe Angenendt, economist at BHF-Bank in Frankfurt, referring to the lower number of workdays.

Economists said if the 2.8 percent adjusted pace gives the more accurate picture of the economy in the first quarter, that could mean Germany may indeed be on course to reach the government's 2.5 percent 1997 growth forecast.
"Growth for the rest of the year may surprise on the upside," said Sonja Gibbs at Nomura International in London.
"Depending on the composition of GDP, we could see a little bit stronger growth than the markets have been anticipating, which could be good for the tax revenue position in Germany," she said.
